title: File sync
like: a file sync app like Dropbox
brief: A folder on your laptop mirrors to the cloud and to your other devices. Small changes must arrive quickly, big files must upload reliably, and a shared folder with thousands of people must not melt the metadata service.

clarify.q: What are the two kinds of data?
clarify.a: File contents (large, in blocks) and file lists with names and versions (small, but constantly changing). They are stored differently.

clarify.q: What happens when two people change the same file?
clarify.a: Keep both versions and show a "conflicted copy". Never silently lose someone's work.

clarify.q: How fast must a change show up on another device?
clarify.a: Within a few seconds for small files. While a part of the service is being repaired, changes may wait in line up to half an hour; later than that counts as failed.

notes: Files are cut into blocks of about 4 MB, and identical blocks are stored once (approx.).
Shared folders are the hot spots.

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Block uploads per second at peak
Storage after dedupe
numbers.how: 3 million people × 0.3 GB after identical blocks are stored once ≈ 900 TB (approx.)

hints: File blocks and file lists are different problems. Do they belong in the same database?
Blocks go to object storage through the CDN; the file list goes to a database that you can split by user.
Garbage collection must respect devices that can still replay old state. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Split the system in two. Blocks are big, immutable and cheap: object storage behind a CDN. The file list is small but changes all the time and needs correctness: a sharded SQL database with versions. A socket tells other devices to look.

designs.name: Blocks in object storage, metadata sharded
designs.why: Uploads and downloads of blocks never touch your servers. Only small metadata calls do. Sharding by user spreads the load, and a socket gateway pushes "something changed" instead of devices polling. Logs, traces and dashboards cut the time to find and free a full disk from about half an hour to about 20 minutes (approx.), and the queue lets sync writes wait meanwhile.

tradeoffs: Storing identical blocks once saves a lot of space but means a block is only deleted when nobody uses it.
Sharding by user spreads load. A shared folder with thousands of people becomes a hot spot that needs its own cache.
Keeping both versions of a conflict is slightly messy but never loses work.
Old file versions can move to cheaper storage: slower to restore, much cheaper to keep.
editorial.realWorld: Sync services keep exabytes of data. Object storage costs roughly $0.02 per GB each month, and metadata databases are sharded into thousands of pieces (approx.).

correctness.prompt: File sync: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Resume chunk uploads and preserve concurrent file versions across devices. Stable upload identity avoids duplicate versions and permits bounded resume. Arrival order cannot decide which independent edit is expendable. Garbage collection must respect devices that can still replay old state.

fields.label: Step 1. A large upload disconnects after three chunks. What retries?
options: The same upload manifest and missing content-addressed chunks
The whole file under a new logical edit every time
fields.explanation: Stable upload identity avoids duplicate versions and permits bounded resume.

fields.label: Step 2. Two laptops edit file version 7 offline. What becomes version 8?
options: Silently keep the last network arrival
Detect the common base and preserve a conflict or perform a defined merge
fields.explanation: Arrival order cannot decide which independent edit is expendable.

fields.label: Step 3. A delete syncs before an old laptop returns. What prevents resurrection?
options: A retained tombstone or deletion epoch and a supported offline horizon
Immediate removal of every trace of the file id
fields.explanation: Garbage collection must respect devices that can still replay old state.

correctness.responsibility: Resume chunk uploads and preserve concurrent file versions across devices.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 1,000 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $35,916. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
